The condition is stability against *unilateral* deviations and nothing more: it does not ask that the outcome be good for anyone (game-1.4), and it says nothing about how players get there. One reading is a steady state of players who have learned what others typically do and have no reason to change; another is a self-enforcing agreement — if everyone expects $a^*$, nobody wants to break it. Checking a cell takes one look down its column and one along its row. The arrows of profitable deviations form a directed graph on the cells whose sinks are exactly the equilibria. In a random $m\times n$ game with continuous payoffs, each cell is a best reply for player 1 with probability $1/m$ and for player 2 with probability $1/n$, independently, so the expected number of pure equilibria is exactly $mn\cdot\frac1m\cdot\frac1n = 1$, and the chance that there is none tends to $1/e$ (Dresher, 1970). Existence in general needs mixed strategies (game-2.3).

For the random-game calculation, take the two payoff arrays independently, with independent identically distributed continuous entries within each array. The indicator of each cell being a mutual best reply has mean $1/(mn)$; linearity of expectation (prob 1.6.1) then gives expected equilibrium count one without assuming that the cell indicators are independent. For the no-equilibrium probability, use the finite uniform space of column maxima for player 1 and row maxima for player 2. Only sets of cells in distinct rows and columns can all be equilibria. There are $\binom mk\binom nk k!$ such k-cell sets, each with joint probability $(mn)^{-k}$. Inclusion–exclusion (comb 3.1), dividing finite event counts by the size of this uniform space, gives the alternating sum of these intersection probabilities. When both m and n grow, its kth term tends to $(-1)^k/k!$ and its absolute value is at most $1/k!$; summable tails give the limit $1/e$. These hypotheses exclude tied discrete-payoff tables and arbitrary dependent continuous arrays.

fields.before: The gain $g_i^a$ measures how much better the pure action $a$ is than the player's current mixture; $f$ shifts weight toward actions that do better. A profile is fixed by $f$ iff all gains vanish: if some gain were positive, then by the linearity of $U_i$ (game-2.1) some action in the support does *worse* than average, loses weight and the point moves; so a fixed point has no profitable deviation (game-2.2). The map is continuous (gains are continuous) and $\Delta$ is compact and convex, so Brouwer (top-13.11, and its set-valued cousin in game-2.4) applies. Mixing is what supplies the convex, compact $\Delta$: with pure strategies only, Matching Pennies has no fixed point (game-1.6).

Let $A$ be a $2\times n$ matrix and let the row player play row 1 with probability $p\in[0,1]$. Against column $j$ she receives
$$L_j(p)=p\,a_{1j}+(1-p)\,a_{2j},$$
a line in $p$. Against a column player who chooses the worst column, her guarantee is the **lower envelope** $g(p)=\min_jL_j(p)$, a concave piecewise-linear function. The **value** is $v=\max_{p\in[0,1]}g(p)$ (game-3.3) and the maximiser $p^*$ is an optimal strategy. At $p^*$ either the maximum is at an end point of $[0,1]$ or it is a crossing of two lines of opposite slope; the columns whose lines pass through the peak form the support of an optimal $y^*$, which mixes (at most) two of them so that the row player is indifferent between her rows. An analogous construction with $m\times2$ games uses the upper envelope.

Let $A$ be a $2\times n$ matrix and let the row player play row 1 with probability $p\in[0,1]$. Against column $j$ she receives
$$L_j(p)=p\,a_{1j}+(1-p)\,a_{2j},$$
a line in $p$. Against a column player who chooses the worst column, her guarantee is the **lower envelope** $g(p)=\min_jL_j(p)$, a concave piecewise-linear function. The **value** is $v=\max_{p\in[0,1]}g(p)$ (game-3.3) and the maximiser $p^*$ is an optimal strategy. An optimum can always be chosen among the interval endpoints and intersections of nonparallel payoff lines, although a flat segment can give a whole interval of optima. At an interior optimum the active lines' slopes have zero in their convex hull, so an optimal column mixture can use at most two active lines and makes the row player indifferent between her rows. A constant active line can suffice by itself. At an endpoint optimum, the unused row need not be indifferent; the appropriate one-sided payoff inequality suffices. An analogous construction with $m\times2$ games uses the upper envelope.

fields.before:
Fixing $p$, the column player's best reply to the row mixture is a pure column (a minimum of linear functions over the simplex is attained at a vertex), so the guarantee is the lower envelope of $n$ lines, and the row player's problem is to find its highest point, a one-dimensional LP. The peak of a concave piecewise-linear function sits at a vertex of the envelope: either an end of the interval or a crossing of a rising line and a falling line. Mixing those two columns with weights that make the two rows pay equally yields a column strategy whose ceiling is exactly the peak height, so the two security levels agree, a hands-on view of the minimax theorem for a $2\times n$ game.

The pointwise-maximum rule opt 3.6 applies to $-g(p)=\max_j[-L_j(p)]$, a finite maximum of affine convex functions, making g concave. This proves the lower-envelope shape used by the graphical optimizer without differentiability at line crossings. An endpoint/intersection candidate list can contain an optimum even when a flat segment gives a whole interval of optima or a constant active line attains the peak; concavity does not require uniqueness or two strictly opposite slopes. The analogous upper envelope is convex.

fields.before: Each column is a line over $p$, drawn through two draggable handles: the left one at $p=0$ gives the payoff if the row player plays row 2, the right one at $p=1$ gives the payoff for row 1. The bold curve is the lower envelope $g(p)$; its summit is the value, marked in green. Lines through the summit are the column player's support. Drag the handles to change the game, change the number of columns, or drag the gold point along $p$ to read the guarantee. Make the summit sit at an end point to see a pure optimum.

Track the potential $\Phi_t=\ln\sum_i e^{\eta G_t(i)}$ with $G_t(i)$ the cumulative gain. Each round raises it by at most $\eta\,x_t\!\cdot g_t+\eta^2/8$ (Hoeffding's lemma), while at the end $\Phi_T\ge\eta\max_iG_T(i)$ and at the start $\Phi_0=\ln m$; rearranging yields the regret bound. For the game, regret against the best fixed row says: the row player did as well as the best row against the *actual* column play, which is the time average $\bar y_T$, so $\max_i(A\bar y_T)_i\le\frac1T\sum_t x_t^{\mathsf T}Ay_t+R^{\rm row}_T/T$; the symmetric bound for the column player and $\sum_tx_t^{\mathsf T}Ay_t$ cancelling gives the displayed $\varepsilon$. The averages converge; the individual iterates $x_t$ generally keep orbiting the optimum, as in game-3.6.

Use the bounded-variable exponential lemma in the proof of stat 1.16, rather than its independent-sample tail conclusion. At a single round introduce an auxiliary action index I with distribution $x_t$, so $g_t(I)\in[0,1]$. That lemma bounds its logarithmic moment generating function by $\eta x_t\cdot g_t+\eta^2/8$, exactly the potential increment used here. It is a one-round inequality for the realized gain vector; temporal independence of gains is unnecessary, even for adaptive full-information play. Summing these increments gives the stated finite-horizon bound, and the choice of eta depending on T makes the averaged minimax gap vanish rather than identifying a unique limiting strategy vector.
